title: Pioneer Health - onprem airgapped discovery
next_steps: Redwood to send on-prem/security spec pack and SOC2/ISO artifact links
Customer to share list of approved HW SKUs and procurement timeline
Schedule a 2-hour benchmark session in Pioneer lab w/ sample prompts (target: within 3 weeks)
action_items: Marco - prepare benchmark plan and cost estimate by 2026-09-22
Sofia - send pricing sheet and security pack by EOD 2026-09-11
Tom - share internal PCI/HIPAA network diagram and approved GPU SKUs by 2026-09-18
summary: Discovery call about on-prem, air-gapped Redwood Private deployment for Pioneer Health. Customer emphasized regulatory constraints (HIPAA, internal audit), offline update process, approved hardware, and strict network isolation. Discussed options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), fallback strategies, kernel/quantization tradeoffs, and pilot/benchmark next steps.
topics: air-gapped update workflow and offline packages
key management (KMS/HSM) and encryption at rest
latency vs unit cost tradeoffs and batching
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia, account executive for Redwood Inference. We also have Marco from the solutions engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Jill: Good, thanks.
[00:12] Tom: Hi.
[00:14] Marco (Redwood): Morning, all. Quick agenda: understand your constraints for an on-prem air-gapped deployment, hardware list, update cadence, and what success looks like for a pilot.
[00:25] Jill: Perfect. Our main ask up front: we're a healthcare provider, so HIPAA and internal audit rules mean we need zero egress, full audit trail, and air-gapped updates. We can't have outbound calls to the public internet from the inference nodes.
[00:39] Sofia (Redwood): Totally understood. We do a lot of work with regulated customers — Redwood Private supports VPC and true on-prem, and we have an air-gapped mode. Marco, want to say a bit about how that looks operationally?
[00:50] Marco (Redwood): Sure. In air-gapped deployments we provide an offline install bundle: container images, model artifacts, and a signed update manifest. The customer or our on-prem team transfers those to the isolated network via removable media or an internal transfer server. The runtime validates signatures against the customer's trusted certs, and we can integrate with HSM/KMS for key material so private keys never leave their environment.
[01:12] Tom: A couple of clarifying points — one, how big are these bundles? Our procurement has limits on how big a drive we can move around and security scans must be run. Two, what is required from our side to validate images?
[01:25] Marco (Redwood): Good questions. For a single model and runtime it's typically a few tens of gigabytes — model weights are the largest piece. Quantized 4-bit versions are much smaller. We can provide incremental diffs for updates to reduce transfer sizes. Validation is signature-based; we sign with Redwood's code signing key and you verify with your rootcert. We can also support customer-signed manifests if you want full control.
[01:44] Jill: Can you support on-prem HSM specifically? Our compliance team requires FIPS 140-2 compliant key storage for any encryption keys.
[01:52] Marco (Redwood): Yes, we've integrated with common HSMs (AWS CloudHSM in private deployments, Thales, Vault HSM backends). In a fully air-gapped scenario we can use a local HSM or an HSM appliance; we just need the integration info.
[02:05] Anika (Compliance): From audit side, we need immutable audit logs for inference requests, admin actions, and update events. How detailed are your logs and can they be exported to our SIEM?
[02:15] Marco (Redwood): Logs include token-level cost/latency per request, request IDs, model version, route, and user IDs if you supply them. We can export via syslog or push to an internal collector; all logs can be set to append-only and signed. In air-gapped mode we ship log forwarders you run inside the network.
[02:30] Jill: What about model provenance — we need to prove the model we used hasn't been tampered with and shows the exact training/quantization metadata.
[02:38] Marco (Redwood): Each model artifact includes a provenance blob: model commit hash, quantization profile, kernel/optimizations applied, and a signed manifest. We also keep a digest you can verify offline. Sometimes customers store that digest in their internal artifact repo for audit.
[02:51] Tom: Hardware — our procurement has approval for A100 40GB and H100, but we have a long lead time on H100s. Does Redwood support mixed clusters, and what are perf implications?
[03:03] Marco (Redwood): Yes, mixed clusters are supported. The runtime can group similar hardware into pools. H100s offer faster throughput and better perf at high batch sizes; A100s are still solid for latency-sensitive workloads. We can also run heterogeneous scheduling: lower-priority or background workloads on older cards.
[03:21] Jill: Are there compatibility limitations for quantized weights or kernels on certain cards? We had an experience where quantized ops weren't optimized on older drivers.
[03:30] Marco (Redwood): There can be kernel or cuDNN/cuBLAS driver mismatches. We recommend pinned driver/kernel versions. Our distro includes validated kernels for the supported SKUs; we provide a driver manifest. For 4-bit quantization we ship optimized kernels for Ampere and Hopper, but if you have very old CUDA stacks we might need a compatibility layer — that can impact perf.
[03:50] Tom: Good to know. Networking question: we will have zero egress from the compute cluster but we do allow an internal management subnet where jump hosts can pull updates from a USB import station — is that pattern supported?
[04:03] Sofia (Redwood): Yes, that's a common pattern. The updates are staged through a hardened bastion that has controlled access to the air-gapped zone. We provide recommended hardening docs.
[04:12] Anika (Compliance): Patch cadence — how often do you push security patches, and how does that map to air-gapped customers? We need a predictable cadence for change control boards.
[04:22] Marco (Redwood): We publish a monthly security bulletin and critical patches as needed. For air-gapped customers, we provide an offline patch bundle and a clear CVE list. You can choose expedited patching for critical CVEs or a quarterly bundled approach — that policy is part of the SOW.
[04:37] Jill: Pilot scope — we want to run a pilot that demonstrates latency SLOs for our triage use case and verifies no data leaves the network. Ideally run with a subset of staff and a red-team scan. Can you do that?
[04:49] Marco (Redwood): Absolutely. Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: we help install the runtime, load a sample model (we can use an open model you approve or your internal model), run ingress traffic patterns, and measure latencies and throughput. We'll also run the offline update flow. For red-team scans we coordinate with your security team to re-sign artifacts if they alter them.
[05:06] Tom: About models — we have proprietary models and may also want Redwood-curated open models. How do licensing and model updates work?
[05:15] Sofia (Redwood): For customer models, you control the artifacts. Redwood will run the runtime and doesn't get access to private weights in the air-gapped mode. For our curated models, we ship the artifacts as part of the bundle and include license metadata. Updates to curated models are optional; you only accept them via signed manifests.
[05:29] Jill: One practical ask: can you provide a list of approved GPU SKUs and minimum disk/ram per node? Procurement needs specs.
[05:36] Marco (Redwood): We'll send a hardware guide; minimum per-node for medium-load is 1 x A100 40GB with 512GB RAM and ~4TB NVMe for cache/model store. For production we recommend 2 x A100 or H100 with 1TB+ RAM for heavy KV/cache footprints. We'll add an explicit SKU list.
[05:55] Tom: Is NFS okay for model store or do you insist on local NVMe?
[05:59] Marco (Redwood): Local NVMe is preferred for latency-critical inference because of random I/O; NFS can be used for cold storage or model artifacts but will impact startup/first-token times.
[06:09] Jill: Pricing — high level, do you charge per-node or per-token for private on-prem?
[06:15] Sofia (Redwood): Private deployments are typically a platform fee plus a per-node license and optional support tiers. We can structure a pilot with reduced fees. We'll include pricing in the follow-up.
[06:23] Anika: Data residency — all telemetry must remain inside our network unless explicitly allowed. Does Redwood require any telemetry by default?
[06:30] Marco (Redwood): By default hosted collects telemetry; for air-gapped we disable outbound telemetry. We can provide offline metrics exports you ingest into your monitoring stack. Any optional telemetry (e.g., anonymous crash stats) is opt-in and can be disabled.
[06:45] (ambient typing)
[06:48] Jill: Talk me through the cert rotation process. Our policy mandates quarterly rotations and an audit log of who rotated what.
[06:55] Marco (Redwood): Cert rotation is supported; we provide tooling to rotate keys and update manifests. Rotations are recorded in the audit log and can be tied to LDAP / SSO user IDs. For HSM-managed keys, rotation is handled in the HSM and we validate via the signed manifests.
[07:10] Tom: For the pilot we want to simulate peak loads — what tooling do you provide for load generation and how do you measure e2e latency?
[07:19] Marco (Redwood): We have a load harness that can replay traffic with real distributions and prefix caching scenarios. We measure per-token latency, first-token, tail-p99/p999, and end-to-end including network hops. We'll run a few scenarios to show the effect of batching and cache warmup.
[07:36] Jill: A few gotchas we've seen: kernel mismatches cause silent perf regressions, and sometimes fallback to CPU happens unexpectedly when memory is low. How do you surface those?
[07:46] Marco (Redwood): The console exposes per-route metrics and traces, including resource pressure signals and fallback events. We can set automatic fallbacks to lighter model variants with alerts. All fallback events are logged and included in the pilot report.
[07:58] Sofia (Redwood): Quick question — have you evaluated hosted or dedicated already, or are you starting with private as a firm requirement?
[08:06] Jill: We did a proof-of-concept with a hosted API for non-PHI data last year, but for production with PHI we need air-gapped private. Cost is a concern so we want to understand tradeoffs.
[08:17] Sofia (Redwood): Understood. We often recommend a hybrid: non-sensitive workloads in hosted to save cost, and PHI in private. We'll show cost modeling for both.
[08:27] Tom: What about fallback strategy in an outage — can we fail over to another region or to a lower-trust hosted environment?
[08:34] Marco (Redwood): For strict air-gapped customers we usually recommend on-prem HA across datacenters. We can architect a cross-data-center sync with encrypted replications. Fallback to hosted is possible but requires data governance approval because of PHI. Some customers keep a sanitized, non-PHI model in hosted for emergency fallbacks.
[08:52] Anika: Does Redwood provide SOC 2/ISO artifacts and third-party pen test reports?
[08:58] Sofia (Redwood): Yes, we have SOC 2 and ISO artifacts; we'll share redacted reports and our pen-test summaries in the security pack. For air-gapped installs we also provide installation and hardening guides used by our compliance customers.
[09:10] Jill: Great. Any limitations on model size? We have some large LLMs (70B+) but we might prefer quantized smaller variants.
[09:18] Marco (Redwood): We can host very large models but they require more GPU memory and sharding. For 70B models we recommend H100 or multi-GPU sharded deploys. Quantization to 4-bit reduces memory footprint but may slightly affect quality; we'll run evals during pilot to measure.
[09:34] Tom: For sharded models do you require RDMA or can you do NCCL over standard ethernet?
[09:40] Marco (Redwood): RDMA is preferred for lowest latency and best scaling; NCCL over 100GbE can work but with some perf cost. We'll document the network recommendations.
[09:48] Jill: Who will own the day-to-day ops? We have an ops team that will run the infra but want Redwood SRE on call for the pilot.
[09:56] Sofia (Redwood): Our typical engagement is we do install support and handover to your ops team; during pilot we provide SRE on-call. Post-install we offer managed support tiers.
[10:06] Marco (Redwood): Also, we can train your ops team on troubleshooting, kernel pinning, and update flows.
[10:12] (short pause)
[10:15] Jill: A small nit — for the offline bundle, how do you guarantee integrity if someone opens and re-packages?
[10:22] Marco (Redwood): The manifests are signed and include checksums. If someone repackages without resigning, verification will fail. For local red-team tests where artifacts are modified, we provide a process to re-sign with a staging key you control.
[10:34] Tom: Can we run a dry-run where we only do the install and not expose real data?
[10:38] Marco (Redwood): Yes, we do a dry-run installation with synthetic data to validate networking, drivers, and data flows before any PHI is loaded.
[10:46] Jill: Sounds good. On timeline, procurement for H100s may take 10-14 weeks; we may want to start pilot on A100s.
[10:55] Marco (Redwood): That's common. We'll architect the pilot for A100 and show a path to H100 later.
[11:00] Sofia (Redwood): I'll summarize next steps: we'll send a security pack, hardware SKUs, pricing, and a proposed pilot plan. Marco will draft the benchmark plan. Tom will share procurement timeline and network diagram.
[11:12] Anika: One more question: do you support SSO with our IdP and SAML for admin users?
[11:18] Marco (Redwood): Yes, SAML SSO, LDAP, and SCIM for provisioning. We can integrate with your IdP in air-gapped mode via a local IdP connector.
[11:27] Jill: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[11:30] Sofia (Redwood): Thank you — we'll follow up with the docs today.
[11:34] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-IDs and split words from auto-transcription; content paraphrased in places for clarity.
